script.title: Cash Book vs Pass Book
script.caption_hook: Same bank, two balances? Here's why both diaries differ.

lines.say: Same bank, two balances? Which one is right?
Both can be right! One is your diary of the bank, the other is the bank's diary of you.
Business keeps the Cash Book. The bank keeps the Pass Book.
But why would the sides look different?
Every debit in your Cash Book appears as a credit in the Pass Book once the bank records it, and vice versa.
Oh! Like a mirror. Then what about the balances?
A Cash Book debit balance means money at bank. A Pass Book credit balance means the same.
So a Pass Book debit balance is an overdraft?
Yes, the customer owes the bank.
Then why don't the two balances match?
Timing gaps: cheques issued but not presented, and cheques deposited but not yet collected. Also errors in either book.
Bank-only items are charges, interest, direct credits and dishonoured cheques. A BRS explains them all.
Remember, the Pass Book is the mirror book, the bank's view of you.

Checker: Line 6 (voice): 'Every debit in your Cash Book appears as a credit in the Pass Book... and vice versa' is too absolute, and it clashes with Lines 12–13. Errors in either book and items recorded only by the bank (charges, interest, direct credits) don't show up as mirror entries until they are corrected or recorded in the Cash Book. Suggested wording: 'Each deposit or payment you record as a debit or credit in the Cash Book shows on the opposite side in the Pass Book once the bank records it.'

Checker: Line 14 (voice and board 'Pass Book = Mirror Book'): 'Mirror Book' is not a standard accounting term, so students may take it for a formal definition. Suggested wording: 'The Pass Book is a copy of your account as the bank records it. Its entries are the mirror image of the Cash Book's bank column.'
